extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, critics, and novelists studying craft
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying E. M. Forster's critical criteria for judging and producing novels (as presented in his Clark Lectures / Aspects of the Novel). Focuses on definitions, characterization, plot/story distinction, point of view, fantasy/prophecy, pattern and rhythm, and related critical cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel definition (extent)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A fiction in prose of a certain extent" (une fiction en prose d’une certaine etendue). For the purposes of these lectures Forster adds that "the extent should not be less than 50,000 words."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any fictitious prose work over 50,000 words will be treated as a novel for these lectures. Forster invites critics to propose alternatives if they want to include/exclude borderline works (examples listed as problematic: The Pilgrim's Progress, Ulysses, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language/geographical proviso ('English')
rubrics_metrics.description: "'English' we shall of course interpret as written in English, not as published south of the Tweed or east of the Atlantic, or north of the Equator."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing 'English' fiction, interpret the term by language (written in English) rather than by political/geographical limits. Continental novels may be acknowledged for scale of achievement, but Forster mostly limits detailed treatment to works written in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final test — affection
rubrics_metrics.description: "The final test of a novel will be our affection for it," — the emotional test, analogous to how we judge friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical judgement ultimately rests on the reader's affection for a novel. This is a 'man-to-man' human test rather than a purely formal or scholastic one; affection can override strictly technical criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story vs. Plot (two distinct concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster distinguishes Story (a sequence of events in time, a 'chronological' narrative) from Plot (events linked by cause and effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work is primarily a story (events told in temporal sequence) or a plot (arranged by causal relationships). The distinction alters what the novelist is trying to achieve and how success should be measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: People / Characters — flat vs round
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters may be 'flat' (constructed around a single idea and not subject to development) or 'round' (capable of real change, surprise, and complexity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples Forster gives: flat characters work well for comedy, types, and certain structural functions; round characters are necessary when the novelist aims to present living human beings. Evaluate whether the chosen type suits the novel's aims. Look for capacity for surprise, inner consistency, and development as markers of 'roundness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / Tone (personal vs impersonal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view and tone shape a novel's effect; Forster notes a basic classification into personal and impersonal tones and stresses the importance of consistent and appropriate narrative viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the narrator's stance, reliability, and the deployment of reported speech devices (e.g., 'he said'/'she said' usage) which vary historically. Inconsistency of point of view or an inappropriate tone (personal/impersonal mismatch) weakens a novel's control and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character space — 'give human beings a good run'
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's problem is 'to give [human beings] a good run and to achieve something else at the same time.' Human beings must 'come in' — the novel must recreate living people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the novel on whether it allows characters freedom to act, develop, surprise, and appear lifelike; also judge how well these human portrayals coexist with any larger artistic aims the novel pursues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy as a mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy (exemplified by Sterne and Virginia Woolf) starts from small objects, takes flights ('a flutter'), combines humour and a sense of life's muddle with appreciation of beauty; it often uses deliberate bewilderment of voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a novel employs fantasy, evaluate how the technique (playfulness, digression, focus on small objects) serves the book's aims. Recognize tonal cousins (Sterne–Woolf) and differences (scale, sentimentality). Fantasy's success depends on maintaining the right tone and not degenerating into mere confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy (novel as prophetic utterance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster treats 'prophecy' as an aspect whereby novels may express a vision or forecast about human nature or society — a novel's persuasive power to reveal larger truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge prophetic claims on plausibility, subtlety, and whether the prophetic element arises from the novel's character portrayals and patterns rather than didactic assertion. Forster devotes a chapter to analyzing how successful 'prophecy' differs from mere topical moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern and Rhythm — repetition plus variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm in fiction can be defined as 'repetition plus variation.' There are two kinds of rhythm: an easy 'diddidy-dum' repetition that adds beauty, and a more complex, large-scale 'rhythmic' relation akin to a symphony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for recurring motifs, phrases, images (Forster's example: Proust's 'little phrase' of Vinteuil) that wax and wane to stitch a book together from the inside. Good rhythm surprises and refreshes; bad rhythm hardens into boring symbol or banner (e.g., Meredith's repeated cherry trees, Galsworthy's endlessly recurring spaniel), which trips the reader up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal stitching (motif vs banner distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motifs that develop and vary (e.g., Proust's little musical phrase) can 'stitch' a book internally; mere banners or repeated symbols that do not develop act as external, static devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value motifs that gain meaning through transformation and reappearance; be wary of repeated images used as crude signposts. Effective internal stitching gives the novel a sense of a homogeneous world without forcing symbolic repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitiveness over topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel's success 'lies in its own sensitiveness, not in the success of its subject matter.' Topical events do not by themselves make a novel better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a novel, distinguish the author's sensibility (ability to perceive and render subtleties of life) from the topical interest of its subject. A great theme or political event does not guarantee artistic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pseudo‑scholarship (against overclassification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics should avoid classifying novels by chronology, subject-matter, or convenient taxonomies without having read them properly; pseudo-scholars 'class books before he has understood or read them' and lean on labels like 'tendency' or 'genius.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical evaluation should be grounded in careful reading and attention to the work itself rather than schematic periodization or fashionable categories (e.g., 'novel of the Women’s Movement,' 'the literature of the weather'). Classification is useful only when supported by intimate knowledge of texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm pitfalls — symbol hardening / boring repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm done badly becomes boring; it 'hardens into a symbol' and trips the reader up rather than carrying them along.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for repeated devices that cease to surprise. If a recurring image, object, or motif appears too often without variation or development (e.g., an author's recurring pet or stock image), treat it as a failing of technique rather than a successful unifying device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of technique and inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster emphasizes that books must be read; technique and tradition vary across generations, and genius/inspiration alone is not an adequate explanation — the critic must attend to actual reading and the 'novelist’s touch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both the craftsmanship (technique, use of point of view, patterning) and the presence of inspiration. Do not rely on invoking 'genius' as a substitute for concrete analysis; specific examples of technique should ground critical judgements.
